Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan , before flying outside the plane of the solar system. A Microsoft service didn’t control the dosing system itself. Unlucky guests who visited the pool complained of respiratory irritation, with four requiring hospitalization. At least forty first responders were dispatched to the initial poisoning incident, according to the local fire department . Instead, it’s an ultra compact object called a neutron star whose mass appears to be on the upper limit of what’s thought to be possible. Neutron stars are the remnants of what used to be a much more massive star that exploded in a supernova . The catastrophic event leaves behind only the star’s incredibly dense core. Though they’re roughly only the size of a human city, their material is so tightly packed that a single tablespoon of the stuff would weigh more than a billion tons. candidates.title: JPMorgan software bug triggers banking delays across US
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Thousands of customers across the United States reported difficulties accessing banking services and completing transactions on Monday, following a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that caused delays involving multiple financial institutions.

Customers reported problems with online and mobile banking services at several major banks, including Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank. Some also experienced delays when sending or receiving payments through Zelle, a popular peer-to-peer payment service.

JPMorgan Chase confirmed that a temporary software bug in its on-premise hardware systems had slowed the processing of some transactions. The bank said customers could still access their accounts and funds, and there was no evidence that the issue was related to a cyberattack.

The disruption had knock-on effects on other financial institutions when they were involved in transactions with Chase.

However, the bank stressed that the incident was not systemic. US Bank said its own systems were not directly affected, while some customers might experience delays with cross-bank Zelle payments. Early Warning Services, Zelle's operator, confirmed that its payment network remained fully operational.

The situation improved later on Monday. At around 6:30 p.m. Eastern Time, a Chase spokesperson said that transactions were posting normally again, indicating that the main disruption had been resolved.

candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials. They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster . The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA. It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there. (Image credit: SETI) Why it mattered The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute. "The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's." This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond. Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA. Although the term light-day might sound like a measurement of time, it is actually a unit of distance, much like a light-year . Astronomers use light-based measurements because conventional miles and kilometers become increasingly difficult to comprehend when describing the enormous distances between objects in space. For perspective on how far Voyager 1 has travelled, sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning our planet is approximately 8.3 light-minutes from the sun. Radio signals traveling between Earth and Mars can take anywhere from three to 22 minutes, depending on the planets' positions in their orbits, according to the statement. By comparison, when Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth , a radio signal sent from the probe will take a full 24 hours to reach mission controllers on Earth, and a command transmitted from Earth will take another 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. candidates.raw_excerpt: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026! When is the best time to look for Leonid meteors? The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere . By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors. Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark. Why are the Leonids special? As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors , which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space. A ship's log is a legally required original record of a vessel's voyage and serves as a key basis for maritime investigations, accident tracing and liability determination.

At the start of the mission, the Super Heavy booster and Starship separated from each other about 2 minutes and 30 seconds into the mission. SpaceX was planning to attempt a catch of the Super Heavy booster, but reported that the boostback burn ended early due to an anomaly. The booster was diverted to an offshore landing in the Gulf and was seen exploding while it splashed down. On the ship side, Starship successfully performed an orbital insertion burn, successfully reaching orbit for the second time after first hitting the milestone in September . Starship then spent more than 21 hours in orbit. During that time it deployed 26 satellites for the Starlink V3 broadband constellation. SpaceX made the determination to return Starship to Earth and attempt the catch, which previous Starship flights have not been able to do. candidates.raw_excerpt: A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket suffered an anomaly during its first launch for the Amazon Leo constellation on Sunday, in a return to flight mission after months out of service. The Vulcan rocket was carrying 40 Amazon Leo satellites, the most in one single launch so far for the constellation. The mission took off at 12:40 p.m. ET on Sunday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The launch broadcast showed the vehicle cleaning the pad and all solid rocket boosters jettisoned about a minute and a half into the mission. The booster engine successfully cut off, and the upper stage engine ignited successfully, about five minutes into the mission. The launch broadcast confirmed the payload fairing was jettisoned. The mission seemed to be on track during the last update around 9 minutes and 30 seconds into the mission, but the launch broadcast ended before announcing the anomaly. ULA said in a statement Sunday afternoon that the Vulcan vehicle “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” This is the first full launch failure for ULA. ULA has not shared further details on the anomaly at this time. The next milestone was set to be Centaur first main engine cut off, at around 17 minutes into the mission. “ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us. That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. candidates.title: Vulcan’s Return-to-Flight Fails
candidates.raw_excerpt: The United Launch Alliance’s eagerly awaited return-to-flight of the Vulcan rocket today did not go as planned. An anomaly 10 minutes after launch meant the 40 Amazon Leo satellites did not reach orbit. ULA is investigating what went wrong. It is the first total failure in ULA’s history. This was just the fifth launch of Vulcan since the first in January 2024 . That was a great success, but since then only one other launch, the third , went as planned. On flights two and four , in 2024 and 2026 respectively, nozzles on the Northrop Grumman Solid Rocket Boosters (SRBs) malfunctioned. Although Vulcan’s core stage compensated for the underperformance and delivered the payloads to their intended destinations, the U.S. Space Force has been hesitant to use Vulcan for its most precious satellites. Several launches have been shifted to SpaceX, although the intent is to reassign some SpaceX missions back to ULA to keep the number of launches per company the same. ULA has a large backlog of commercial satellite orders including many for Amazon’s satellite internet constellation Amazon Leo. Today was intended to demonstrate Vulcan is ready for both commercial and government payloads. Vulcan is replacing ULA’s Delta and Atlas V rockets. The final Delta IV launched in 2024 . Six Atlas Vs remain, but are under contract to Boeing for Starliner. Vulcan is ULA’s future. Today’s launch was originally scheduled for Friday, but scrubbed by a pump failure at Air Liquide’s gaseous nitrogen (GN2) plant. Rescheduled for yesterday, that was postponed due to a network communication issue between ground equipment and the launch vehicle. Today’s liftoff at 12:11 pm ET slipped to the end of the 29-minute window because of oscillations in a liquid hydrogen pressure relief valve. candidates.title: ULA suffers first outright failure with loss of Vulcan rocket carrying 40 Amazon Leo satellites
candidates.raw_excerpt: A United Launch Alliance Vulcan, equipped with six solid rocket boosters, lifts off from Cape Canaveral’s pad 41. A failure 10 minutes into flight resulted in the loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites. Image: Michael Cain/Spaceflight Now In a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the company’s new heavy-lift Vulcan rocket carrying a batch of Amazon Leo internet satellites, malfunctioned during the climb to space Sunday, dooming the payload and throwing a costly wrench into the launch schedule of both companies. “Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 (at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station) suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit,” ULA said in a statement some 50 minutes after liftoff. “We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action and return to flight as quickly as possible.” It was the first outright failure of a United Launch Alliance rocket since the company, a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, was formed in 2006. It wasn’t immediately known what went wrong, but the Vulcan, the rocket replacing ULA’s fleet of Atlas 5 rockets, will face a potentially significant grounding while engineers review telemetry and implement fixes for whatever caused the mishap.
